# Rental market {#sec-rental}

## Median rent has climbed fastest since 2019, in every locality


::: {.cell layout-align="left"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Median rent has climbed fastest since 2019, in every locality](rental_files/figure-html/fig-median-rent-1.png){#fig-median-rent fig-align='left' fig-alt='Grouped horizontal bar chart of median gross rent for the four primary Richmond-area localities and Virginia in 2014, 2019, and 2024, in nominal dollars. The 2014 bars are muted grey. Every locality\'s 2024 bar is well above its 2019 bar. Richmond city remains below the statewide median in 2024.' width=100%}
:::
:::


- **Every primary locality posted a higher median gross rent in 2024 than in 2019, and in all four the 2019-to-2024 increase outpaced the full 2014-to-2019 span.**
- Chesterfield had the highest 2024 median gross rent among the four primary localities at $1,629.
- Richmond city's median rent rose 34 percent since 2019, from $1,025 to $1,372 — yet stayed below the statewide median of $1,579.
- All figures are nominal dollars; inflation-adjusted comparisons come with the cost-burden analysis.

## Renter shares held steady since 2019, except in the smallest counties


::: {.cell layout-align="left"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Renter shares held steady since 2019, except in the smallest counties](rental_files/figure-html/fig-renter-share-1.png){#fig-renter-share fig-align='left' fig-alt='Dumbbell chart comparing the renter share of households in 2019 and 2024 for the four primary Richmond-area localities and Virginia. Richmond city has by far the highest renter share, near 57 percent in both years. Henrico is near 36 percent in both years, and Virginia near 33 percent. Chesterfield and Hanover are both below 25 percent.' width=100%}
:::
:::


- **The region added roughly 11,090 renter households between 2019 and 2024, a 8% increase — faster growth than the full prior five years.**
- Richmond city drove the gain, adding about 7,107 renter households since 2019 — roughly NA of the regional increase — though its renter share held near 56% because total households grew just as fast.
- Chesterfield and Hanover renter counts grew steadily since 2019, but both counties remain more than three-quarters owner-occupied.
- Over the full decade, the region added 20,493 renter households (16%) — most of that growth came in the last five years.

## Asking rents are up 28 percent since 2020, even as the market has loosened


::: {.cell layout-align="left"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Asking rents are up 28 percent since 2020, even as the market has loosened](rental_files/figure-html/fig-costar-rent-1.png){#fig-costar-rent fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of the average multifamily asking rent per unit in the eight-locality Richmond region, quarterly from 2020 through mid-2026, in nominal dollars, with a shaded band marking 2022 onward. The line rises from about $1,235 in early 2020 to $1,422 by early 2022 — the market\'s tightest point, with vacancy near 5.6 percent — then keeps climbing to $1,583 by the second quarter of 2026, even as vacancy rises to 8.5 percent.' width=100%}
:::
:::


- **Regional average asking rent reached $1,583 in 2026 Q2, up 28% from $1,235 in early 2020.**
- The market was tightest in early 2022 — vacancy near 6%, the low point of the period — and rents have risen another 11% since then, to $1,583.
- Vacancy has since climbed to 8.5% in 2026 Q2, above where it stood at the start of 2020, as new deliveries caught up with and then outpaced demand.

::: {.callout-note}
## Since 2022
The 2022 Framework flagged a regional average asking rent of $1,395 in early 2022 as a two-decade high with vacancy near 5%. Rents have since risen another 11% to $1,583, but the market has loosened: vacancy is now 8.5%, and rent growth has slowed sharply. The 2022 Framework also reported a net *loss* of renter households from 2016 to 2020 (with a COVID-era data caveat); the 2020–2024 ACS instead shows renter households growing across the region.
:::

## Nearly 30 percent of the region's assisted units expire within a decade


::: {.cell layout-align="left"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Nearly 30 percent of the region's assisted units expire within a decade](rental_files/figure-html/fig-nhpd-risk-1.png){#fig-nhpd-risk fig-align='left' fig-alt='Column chart of active federally assisted rental units in the Richmond region by subsidy-expiration window. About 2,142 units expire 2026-2030, 4,349 expire 2031-2035, 3,982 expire 2036-2040, 8,972 expire 2041 or later, and 3,336 carry no listed expiration date, mostly public housing and HOME-assisted properties.' width=100%}
:::
:::


- **About 6,491 of the region's 22,745 active assisted units — 29% — carry subsidies expiring by 2035, the window preservation funders typically prioritize.**
- Three-quarters of tracked properties (152 of 201) are LIHTC-financed, holding 17,465 units; LIHTC's own affordability period can lapse independently of the subsidy end date tracked here, a second layer of risk this figure does not fully capture.
- Richmond city and Henrico account for the large majority of tracked properties in the four primary localities; Chesterfield and Hanover have smaller inventories.
- About 3,336 units carry no listed subsidy end date, mostly public housing and HOME-assisted properties whose affordability commitments do not lapse the same way project-based subsidies do.

## Housing Choice Vouchers grew as public housing kept shrinking


::: {.cell layout-align="left"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Housing Choice Vouchers grew as public housing kept shrinking](rental_files/figure-html/fig-psh-mix-1.png){#fig-psh-mix fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of regional federal rental-assistance units, 2020 through 2024, for two programs. Housing Choice Vouchers rose from 5,910 to 6,822 units. Public housing fell from 3,706 to 3,226 units. Project-based Section 8 held near 5,770 units and is not plotted here.' width=100%}
:::
:::


- **Housing Choice Vouchers grew 16% since 2020, from 5,879 to 6,795 units, while public housing fell 13%, from 3,706 to 3,226 — a policy-relevant shift from project-based to tenant-based assistance.**
- Regional voucher utilization slipped from 91 percent occupied in 2020 to 87 percent in 2024, even as the voucher supply grew — more vouchers issued, a slightly larger share sitting unused at any given time.
- Project-based Section 8 (5,763 units in 2024) and the small 202/PRAC and 811/PRAC senior- and disability-designated programs (222 and 69 units) have stayed essentially flat since 2020.
- Richmond city and Henrico hold the large majority of the region's assisted units among the four primary localities.
